source_text: Hominis est praeparare cor et a Domino responsio linguae ... ut existiment cor praeparare, hoc est bonum inchoare, sine adiutorio gratiae Dei ad hominem pertinere
pass_a_gloss: 'It is of a human being to prepare the heart, and from the Lord the answer of the tongue' — they so take it that to prepare the heart, that is to begin the good, belongs to the human being without the help of God's grace.

lemmas.lexica: LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'

pass_b_english: Augustine reports that the authors read the saying “It is for a human being to prepare the heart, and the Lord gives the tongue’s answer” as meaning that preparing the heart—that is, beginning something good—belongs to a human being without the help of God’s grace (Proverbs 16:1).

choices.why: In the suum cuique definition gratia is partiality, not saving grace.
Keep Julian's good-of-nature vs good-of-will contrast; do not baptize as 'grace'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

bible_refs.note: Linked from Julian's wording or a clear allusion in the excerpt.

speaker: Julian and fellow bishops (Collective letter to Thessalonica, words preserved in Augustine, Contra duas epistolas Pelagianorum 2–4); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded. This row is Augustine's report; Pass A glosses only the Julian words recoverable here.
